planting.note: Establish on limestone-substrate hammock trees, cork slabs, or rough-barked mounts in partial shade with high humidity; Vanilla dilloniana forms a multi-branched, largely leafless climbing vine that occasionally produces small, fleshy, short-lived leaves near branch tips but otherwise photosynthesizes mainly through its stems and roots. Only grow legally propagated nursery divisions -- wild plants are state-endangered in Florida and protected in the West Indies.

directions: Grow on rough-textured tree bark, cork, or coral-rock mounts in filtered light and warm, humid air -- Dillon's Vanilla is native to coastal berms, limestone hardwood hammocks, and the fringes of mangrove and cypress wetlands across the southern tip of Florida, the Florida Keys, and parts of the West Indies. The many-branched, wiry vine can extend to roughly 15 feet, clasping its supports with aerial roots along a zigzagging stem; true leaves are sparse, small, and fleshy, usually shed by the time the plant flowers, so most of the plant's carbon fixation happens in the green stems and roots rather than in foliage. Pale, waxy flowers open for only part of a single day and, in cultivation away from its native pollinators, need to be hand-pollinated with a fine tool to set the elongated seed pods. Vanilla dilloniana is listed as endangered in Florida due to habitat loss and historic overcollection, so garden specimens should always be sourced from licensed native-plant nurseries propagating legally obtained stock.
sources: Flora of North America -- Vanilla dilloniana treatment

planting.note: Start young plants at the base of a rough-barked tree, cork slab, or trellis in a shaded, humid position; Vanilla phaeantha behaves as a terrestrial seedling at first, rooting into leaf litter, then sends climbing stems up onto bark and eventually becomes a true epiphyte once the original ground-level growth dies back. Source only nursery-propagated material, as wild populations are state-endangered in Florida.

directions: Grow in the humid, shaded conditions of a cypress-swamp or hammock understory, training the vine onto rough bark, cork, or a shaded trellis with consistently moist but well-drained footing -- Leafy Vanilla ranges from South Florida's cypress swamps and hardwood hammocks through the Caribbean and southeastern Mexico into Central America, making it the most widely distributed of Florida's native vanilla orchids. Its stems grow in a distinctive zigzag pattern with a single stout aerial root at each leaf axil, and unlike the mostly leafless V. barbellata and V. dilloniana, it retains oblong, leathery, dark-green leaves for its entire life. Young plants begin life rooted in the forest floor before climbing onto a host tree, after which the original terrestrial stem dies away, leaving a fully epiphytic vine drawing moisture and nutrients from humid air and accumulated leaf litter. Flowers are pale greenish-yellow, open briefly, and require hand pollination in cultivation to produce the narrow seed pods. Vanilla phaeantha is listed as endangered in Florida because of habitat loss and illegal collecting, so cultivated stock should always come from licensed propagators.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants, University of South Florida
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden -- The Florida Vanilla Vine

planting.note: Provide a substantial climbing support such as a large tree, arbor, or wall of cork panels -- Vanilla mexicana is a vigorous, many-branched vine that can eventually reach several meters, considerably larger and leafier than Florida's other native vanilla orchids, with one broad, thin, ovate leaf at every stem node. Hand pollinate flowers for pod set; source only nursery-propagated stock, as wild plants are state-endangered in Florida.

directions: Train onto a large tree, arbor, or extensive cork or bark-covered support in a humid, partly shaded spot with steady moisture and rich organic footing -- Mexican Vanilla is the most widely ranging of the four vanilla species native to Florida, extending from the coastal wetlands, cypress swamps, and hammocks of the state's southeastern edge through the West Indies, Mexico, and Central America into northern South America. It is a much larger, more vigorous vine than its Florida relatives, capable of climbing many meters into the canopy of its host trees, with broad, thin, ovate leaves borne singly at each node along stems that cling by aerial roots. Clusters of up to half a dozen pale greenish flowers open briefly and, without their natural tropical pollinators, must be hand-pollinated to set seed pods. Despite its close kinship to commercial vanilla, cured pods of V. mexicana develop little of the characteristic vanillin fragrance, earning it the alternate names Fuchs' Vanilla and Scentless Vanilla among botanists. In Florida, where it sits at the northern edge of its range, the species is listed as endangered due to habitat loss and illegal collection, so plants for cultivation should come only from licensed native-plant or orchid nurseries.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants, University of South Florida
